title: Part 1.III — Scope and Reduction
summary: Burke's chapter develops two of his most transferable methodological constructs — the *representative anecdote* (the small condensed case that 'contains in nuce the terminological structure that is evolved in conformity with it') and *circumference* (the analyst's elective scope-of-scene, which constrains what motives become visible). Around these he constructs Act as a locus of motives co-equal with Scene, Agent, Agency, and Purpose (book pp.64-69), runs a long pantheism/ontology speculation as the dialectical 'halfway stage' between Creation-doctrine and naturalism (pp.69-77), and applies the apparatus to a sustained case-study of *monetary reduction* (pp.91-126) — money as 'technical substitute for God,' the medium that has supplanted the religious circumference as the public ground of motive in capitalist culture. The chapter closes with the Love/Knowledge/Authority triad (pp.117-124) as a typology of motivational orders that succeeds the simple Virgin/Dynamo binary inherited from Henry Adams.

outline.summary: Sets the chapter's master problem: a vocabulary of motives must be both *representative* (have scope) and *reductive* (have simplicity), avoiding the deflection that ensues when the originating anecdote is not commensurate with the subject. Drama is offered as Burke's representative anecdote for human motives; behaviorist conditioned reflex is the negative example (animal anecdote cannot represent linguistic-symbolic motives).

Extended quotation from a William James letter (via Ralph Perry, vol. 2) on Creation vs. pantheism: James insists creation must contain 'an arbitrary and magical element . . . undetermined by anything external to the agent.' Burke uses this as the entry-point to extract Act as a locus of motives. Footnote warns the reader that the next eleven pages are a 'mull-over' that may be skipped to p.74.

Burke's most explicit argument that Act must be retained as one of five non-reducible motivational loci. The 'Creation' figures here as the *paradigm* or prototype act — the act that is causa sui, that 'has its motive within the creative circumference.' From this paradigm Burke extracts a generalizable claim: *every* act contains a modicum of novelty/magic that cannot be re-located under Scene, Agent, Agency, or Purpose. Proverbs ('l'appétit vient en mangeant', 'Übung macht den Meister'), the writing of a long book, and the poiemata/pathemata/mathemata sequence are deployed as flatland confirmations of the act-locus claim. Spinoza's universal substance as *causa sui* is invoked as philosophic precedent; Coleridge's 'dim analogue of Creation' as poetic.

Pursues the dramatistic embarrassment: if Creation is itself an act, what scene contains it? Burke distinguishes the Thomist position ('God willed the good because it is good' — scenic principle of perseitas boni) from the Scotist/Occamite position ('the good is good because God willed it' — agent principle); reads the controversy as a political-sociological displacement of medieval-vs.-absolutist theories of sovereignty.

The pantheistic temptation: 'Being' as the over-all god-term collapses the Creator/creature ratio into simultaneity (Spinoza's *Deus sive Natura*, *sub specie aeternitatis*). Logical priority replaces temporal priority; what 'always was, is, and will be, must be' — and so the ontological merges the *is*, the *must be*, and the *rational*.

The pantheistic merger of person and scene becomes the bridge from theology to naturalism. The reflexive grammar (Spinoza's *causa sui*, *natura naturans/natura naturata*; Descartes' *res cogitans/res extensa*; Aristotle's active/passive/middle reduction in the *Physics*) supplies the deep grammar by which freedom and necessity, agent and scene, become interchangeable; that interchange in turn licenses naturalism's dissolution of person into impersonal scene.

The chapter's second master construct. 'When defining by location, one may place the object of one's definition in contexts of varying scope.' Burke runs four worked illustrations: (a) the behaviorist's animal-laboratory circumference is itself a 'humanized' scene that imports the very thing it ostensibly excludes; (b) the historical narrowing from a teleological/Creation circumference to an efficient-cause/vis-a-tergo circumference accompanies the shift from Christian theology to modern naturalism; (c) Stark Young's remark on Clifford Odets — that one cannot ask a dramatist 'to surpass his epoch' — is unmasked as a scene-act ratio applied with too narrow a circumference (Shakespeare did 'surpass his epoch'); (d) Mitya Karamazov and Alyosha share an identical Scene that yields radically different motives because each interprets it with a different circumference. The decisive principle: 'a selection of circumference is in itself an act, an act of faith.'

Most workaday writing chooses a circumference 'somewhere between' theology and behaviorism — a 'monographic' or thesis-bound scope. Burke's worked example is James Marshall's *Swords and Symbols*: a competent monograph on political power whose strict terminological self-confinement (force, power, threat, police, appetite, fraud) is wholly proper inside its declared circumference but produces 'a faulty interpretation of motives' when read by the naïve as a statement about the ultimate origin of the ethical. The lesson: a narrow circumference can pass for a wide one if its readers do not recognize the genitive shift from 'a part of' to 'apart from.'

The chapter's long applied case-study begins. The industrial-rationalist narrowing of circumference proceeds in stages: God's law → natural law → environmental/economic factors → monetary/financial. Money 'transubstantiates' from agency (medium of exchange) into ground/purpose of action (the motive that organizes production and distribution). Capitalist 'freedom' is grammatically deducible from a scene whose circumference has shrunk to the monetary market.

Burke disambiguates *three* senses of reduction: (1) reduction of the non-verbal to the verbal ('a cosmology is a reduction of the world to the dimensions of words'); (2) reduction of one terminology to another by translation ('x in terms of y'); (3) reduction in the pejorative sense of lowering or narrowing — Bentham, Occam's Razor, debunking, atomistic 'building-block' philosophies. He notes the third type's hidden 'inverted perfectionism': reductions that claim 'all men are motivated by nothing but greed and fear' attribute to humans the same impossible purity they ostensibly debunked.

Burke's most explicit anti-reductive principle: 'as soon as we encounter a motivational simplicity, we must assume as a matter of course that it contains a diversity.' Worked through a hypothetical Berkeleyan-Thomist universe of consubstantial ideas. Operationalist reductions (Bridgman) drop the over-all god-term entirely, but Burke shows that two men performing the same operations may be performing *different acts* if the surrounding motive-equations differ. Citation of Aquinas (via Bréhier): 'Dieu meut tous les êtres selon le mode de chacun.'

Money is shown to do, in the secular technological scene, exactly the integrative work that 'God' did in the religious-tribal scene — it is the universal symbol, the unitary ground that mediates among an otherwise unmanageable diversity of occupational/private motives. Protestantism's relocation of God to a *private* principle is read as a structural response to money's having occupied the *public* mediating role formerly held by the deity. The shift from 'consistent' humanism ('God's personality, therefore human personality') to 'compensatory' humanism ('nature's impersonality, nevertheless human personality') tracks the grammatical move from a calculus of *therefore* to a calculus of *nevertheless*.

Money is not 'a mere agency' in capitalist culture — it is a rationalizing ground that generates its own 'capitalist psychosis,' a culture-wide recipe of over-stressings and under-stressings. The closing anecdote: a stock-market column equating a hurricane's destruction of physical wealth with a market 'recession's' destruction of symbolic stock-value — the writer instinctively unable to distinguish the two — exposes how thoroughly the monetary circumference becomes 'second nature.' Capitalism, Fascism, and Communism may be three variants of one 'monetary psychosis,' all grounded in technological occupational diversity.

Closing typology: terminological reductions ascend out of historically prominent orders of *power*. Burke expands Henry Adams' Virgin/Dynamo binary into a triad — Love (*ubertas*, biological/tribal order of reproduction and appetite), Knowledge (*veritas*, technological order of intellection and production), Authority (*auctoritas*, order of group cohesion, originator-progenitor-leader). The three orders generate three families of motivational vocabulary; conflicts among them are conflicts among the circumferences each presupposes.

concepts.gloss: The compact case that condenses the analytical pattern Burke will then expand into a full terminology; the form 'in conformity with which the vocabulary is constructed.' A good representative anecdote is to a vocabulary of motives what a paradigm is to a research program — its scope-limiter and its generative seed.
The analyst's elected scope-of-scene; the size of the contextual frame within which an act is located. Burke's most transferable methodological construct after the pentad itself.

Every vocabulary of motives is simultaneously a *scope* (the range of phenomena it intends to cover) and a *reduction* (the simplification by which it makes the range tractable). When the reduction outruns the scope, the vocabulary deflects rather than reflects.
The pathology of a vocabulary whose terminology is not commensurate with its subject — the selection ceases to reflect and becomes a distortion.
Burke's near-synonym for representative anecdote at the level of method: the case 'in nuce' that contains the terminology to be developed from it.
The 'ultimate' or 'consummate' instance of the phenomenon being theorised — Burke's example: the Act of Creation as paradigm of Act in general.
The thesis that Act is not exhaustively reducible to Scene, Agent, Agency, or Purpose; every act contains an irreducible 'modicum of novelty' or 'magic.'
The element in any act that is not derivable from its scene, agent, agency, or purpose — what makes the act a *causa sui*.
Spinoza's term for substance as cause-of-itself; Burke generalizes it as the formal property of any genuine act.
Burke's borrowed William-James phrase for the dialectical halfway-stage between Creation-doctrine and pantheism; the locus where action-language begins to pass into motion-language.
The scenic-pre-condition that the dramatistic logic demands even of God's creative act — the 'pre-first scene' that, when collapsed into the act itself, generates pantheism.

The grammatical move by which Creator and creature, scene and act, freedom and necessity, become 'coequal and coeval' — Spinoza's *Deus sive Natura*. Burke's diagnosis: this merger is the historical bridge from theology to naturalism.
The over-all summarizing term in a vocabulary — the universal title to which all less general terms are related as parts to whole. 'Being,' 'God,' and 'money' are Burke's leading examples.

Burke's observation that pantheism finds its formal expression in *reflexive* verbal forms (natura naturans/naturata; res cogitans/res extensa; active/passive/middle voice) that put scene and agent into one.

The 'two primary generalizations that characterize the quality of motives'; together they signal that one is in the presence of god-terms. Pantheism collapses them; consistent theology keeps them distinct.
Burke's working synonym for circumference; the size of the contextual orbit selected for the location of an act.
Burke's formal pair: every act of placement institutes a 'terministic relationship' between the chosen scope (circumference) and what is placed inside it (the circumscribed).
Burke's striking phrase: the selection of circumference 'is in itself an act, an act of faith.' Circumference-choice is not a methodological preliminary but a constitutive act of the analysis.

The historical-philosophical motion by which a wider motivational scope (e.g., Creator-and-Creation) is replaced by a narrower one (e.g., natural law alone, then environment alone, then monetary scene alone). Burke's structural account of secularisation and reduction-to-materialism.

Most actual writing operates with a 'monographic' circumference — a thesis-bound scope narrower than theology, wider than behaviorism. Misread as a universal claim, the monograph becomes a faulty interpretation of motives.

The case-study of how the historical narrowing of circumference proceeds: God's law → natural law → environment → economic factors → monetary/financial. Money 'transubstantiates' from agency to ground.

Money plays the same integrative public-mediating role in capitalist culture that 'God' played in religious-tribal culture: the unitary symbol in terms of which an otherwise unmanageable diversity of motives is reduced to a common rationale.
The culture-wide 'particular recipe of over-stressings and under-stressings' generated when money becomes the rationalizing ground rather than a mere agency of action.
Burke's threefold typology: (1) non-verbal-to-verbal; (2) one-terminology-to-another; (3) lowering/narrowing (debunking, atomism, materialist reduction).
The error of 'tough-minded' reductions that, in lowering all motives to a single pejorative (greed, fear, lust for power), commit the same purity-of-motive fallacy they accuse idealism of committing.
'As soon as we encounter a motivational simplicity, we must assume that it contains a diversity.' The methodological converse of the representative-anecdote principle.
Motives that are 'simple' in the way chapter-headings are simple — i.e., they name the topic to be filled out, not the analysis of it. The pentad terms themselves are titular in this sense.

Bridgman's program of dropping over-all god-terms in favor of operations-language. Burke notes that two men performing the same operations may yet be performing different acts if their surrounding motive-equations differ.
The doctrine that lets freedom and necessity coexist by deriving them from two distinct sources (Creator vs. Creation), avoiding the pantheistic collapse.
The historically constituted environment (legal, economic, technological) that, in proportion as it is internalized, becomes for its inhabitants as motivationally given as biological nature.

Burke's closing typology of three great orders of power that have stimulated motivational vocabularies: Love/*ubertas* (biological-tribal reproduction), Knowledge/*veritas* (technological-rational production), Authority/*auctoritas* (group cohesion, originator/progenitor/leader).
Henry Adams' pair of motivational orders (natural reproductive forces vs. industrial-mechanical forces); Burke retains it but expands it into the Love/Knowledge/Authority triad.
The structural transition by which money is converted from an *agency* of action into the *ground or purpose* of action — the moment at which it stops being a means and becomes the motive.

methodological_apparatus.name: representative-anecdote
methodological_apparatus.burke_definition_paraphrase: The form, case, or paradigm 'in conformity with which the vocabulary is constructed' — a concentrated instance of the phenomenon to be theorised that contains, in compressed form, the full terminology that will be unfolded from it.

rubric_features.feature: Representativeness — must contain in compressed form the constitutive properties of the class of phenomena it stands for
rubric_features.negative_example: behaviorist conditioned-reflex experiment (animal anecdote cannot represent human linguistic-symbolic motivation)

rubric_features.feature: Scope — must be supple and complex enough to be representative of the subject-matter it is designed to calculate
rubric_features.positive_example: drama as the representative anecdote for human motives — encompasses personality + action + role

rubric_features.feature: Reduction — must simultaneously possess simplicity, i.e., a manageable compression of the subject-matter
rubric_features.discussion: Scope and reduction are not opposed but cooperatively constitutive; the failure-state is *deflection* when the reduction outruns the scope

rubric_features.feature: Containment 'in nuce' — the informative anecdote contains implicitly what the system that is developed from it contains explicitly
rubric_features.discussion: The anecdote is 'a conclusion that follows from the selection of a given anecdote' — i.e., the terminology is internally consistent with its seed

rubric_features.feature: Paradigm/prototype — the analysis should also derive a *consummate* or 'pure' instance of the phenomenon by following the implications of the anecdote to their limit
rubric_features.positive_example: the Act of Creation as the 'pure act,' the prototype of Act in general — useful even if not literally believed, because it lets the analyst discern in lesser acts the qualities the pure case possesses clearly

rubric_features.feature: Conformity-test — if the originating anecdote is not representative, a vocabulary developed in strict conformity with it will not be representative; the giveaway is a 'break in the conformity at some crucial point' (e.g., the behaviorist who induces responses in his fellow experimenters by linguistic appeal while denying that humans are anything but chemicals)
rubric_features.discussion: Burke's diagnostic instrument: check whether the analyst's own practice respects the limits of the anecdote that licenses the vocabulary

burkes_examples.example: drama (Burke's chosen anecdote for human motives)
Act of Creation (paradigm of pure Act)

Goethe's *Die Wahlverwandtschaften* — superficially uses chemical affinity but in fact 'humanizes chemical substance,' a counter-illustration of how a literary work's choice of anecdote is constitutive
conditioned reflex (behaviorist anecdote — negative example: notably informative but not representative)

methodological_apparatus.name: circumference
methodological_apparatus.burke_definition_paraphrase: The scope-of-scene the analyst elects when locating an act for motive-attribution; the implicit or explicit answer to the question 'how big should the scene be?' Different circumferences yield different motives for the same act, because the contextual frame is itself motivationally constitutive.

rubric_features.feature: Circumference selection is itself an act (an 'act of faith') — not a methodological preliminary but a constitutive analytic move
rubric_features.discussion: Once one acknowledges this, the question 'why this scope and not another?' becomes the analyst's primary justificatory burden

rubric_features.feature: The scene-act ratio governs circumference: 'the quality of the context in which a subject is placed will affect the quality of the subject placed in that context'
rubric_features.discussion: A narrower scene yields more mechanistic acts; a wider scene yields more teleological/personal acts

rubric_features.feature: Identifiable ranges — supernatural / natural / second-nature-cultural-historical / temporally-and-geographically-local — each is a distinct circumference and yields a distinct family of motive-attributions
rubric_features.discussion: Burke's working scale: cosmic → natural → cultural-historical → epochal → biographical → episodic

rubric_features.feature: Narrowing-of-circumference is a directional historical motion that accompanies secularization: God's-law → natural-law → environment → economic factors → monetary/financial
rubric_features.discussion: The historical-philosophical mechanism by which a teleological motivational vocabulary is replaced by an efficient-cause / vis-a-tergo / stimulus-response vocabulary

rubric_features.feature: Wider circumference may be poorer in content — the law of formal logic that intension and extension vary inversely; 'world-views' can be the narrowest of all
rubric_features.discussion: Burke's caution against assuming that wider scope automatically means richer motive-attribution; the wider circle can be vacuous

rubric_features.feature: Same-scene-different-circumference test: when two agents inhabit identically the same scene but interpret it with different circumferences, the motives diverge — Mitya and Alyosha Karamazov
rubric_features.discussion: Burke's worked literary example; the test isolates circumference as an independent motivational variable

rubric_features.feature: Monographic-placement test: a deliberately narrow circumference (e.g., 'the technique of sovereignty,' 'material needs as ground of ethics') is proper inside its declared scope but generates 'a faulty interpretation of motives' when the reader mistakes it for a universal claim
rubric_features.discussion: Burke's diagnostic for ideological misuse: a part-of has been silently converted into an apart-from

burkes_examples.example: behaviorist laboratory: animal-circumference applied to humans; ironic exposure when the experiment itself is a 'human' scene
Christian theology → naturalism: narrowing from teleological/Creation circumference to efficient-cause/mechanism
Stark Young on Clifford Odets' *Night Music*: scene-act ratio applied with too narrow a circumference (Shakespeare counterexample)
Mitya vs. Alyosha Karamazov: identical scene, different circumferences, different motives
James Marshall, *Swords and Symbols*: narrow but proper monograph misread as a statement on ultimate origins of the ethical
Monetary reduction: the historical narrowing of motivational circumference from God to money, and the consequent transubstantiation of money from agency to ground
Henry Adams' Virgin/Dynamo: two contrasting circumferences (biological-reproductive vs. technological-productive) each generates its own motive-family

positions: Burke: a vocabulary of motives is constituted by its representative anecdote; the anecdote is not a illustrative addition but the seed-form of the entire terminology.
Burke: Act is a non-reducible locus of motives; every act contains an irreducible 'modicum of novelty' that cannot be relocated under Scene, Agent, Agency, or Purpose without remainder.
Burke: the selection of a circumference is itself an act, an 'act of faith,' and is the constitutive (not merely preliminary) move of any motive-analysis.
Burke: the historical movement from theology to naturalism is grammatically (not just empirically) a narrowing of circumference enabled by the pantheistic merger of agent and scene.

Burke: money in capitalist culture is not a mere agency but a god-term — the public mediating ground that has structurally replaced the religious mediating ground (and therefore made room for Protestantism's relocation of God to a private principle).

Burke: every motivational simplicity contains a diversity; therefore titular reductions ('greed,' 'lust for power,' 'utility') are heuristic chapter-headings whose contents must be filled out, not analytic conclusions.

Burke: the great orders of power that have shaped motivational vocabularies — Love (*ubertas*), Knowledge (*veritas*), Authority (*auctoritas*) — are mutually irreducible; conflicts among them are conflicts among the circumferences each presupposes.

tensions.description: Burke wants Act to be an irreducible motivational locus (containing a 'modicum of novelty'/magic), but the pantheistic grammar he himself analyzes (Spinoza's *causa sui*, the reflexive forms) collapses the act-agent-scene distinction by treating substance as cause-of-itself. The same Spinoza who underwrites Act-as-causa-sui (p.68) is the Spinoza whose *Deus sive Natura* collapses freedom and necessity (p.75). Burke's position requires Spinoza as an ally for one half of the argument and as an interlocutor-to-be-resisted for the other half.

Circumference-selection is itself an act and 'an act of faith' (p.84). But then the very dramatistic vocabulary that includes Act presupposes a circumference within which Act will be a salient term — so the choice of dramatism is itself a circumference-choice that cannot be non-circularly justified from outside dramatism. Burke notes (p.59) that the representative anecdote is 'itself so dramatistic a conception that we might call it the dramatistic approach to dramatism: an introduction to dramatism that is deduced from dramatism, and hence gains plausibility in proportion as dramatism itself is more fully developed' — a candid acknowledgment of the circularity rather than a resolution of it.

Burke's monetary-reduction section moves between two postures: (1) a structural account of money as the legitimate (if reductive) public-mediating term that performs in capitalist culture the integrative work formerly done by God; (2) a critical diagnosis of the 'capitalist psychosis' that makes a hurricane and a stock-market loss appear analogous. The first posture grants money its grammatical role; the second exposes that role as motivational distortion. Burke does not fully reconcile the two registers.
tensions.burke_acknowledges: partially (he hedges with 'we may legitimately isolate the monetary motive as an essence' on p.114)

tensions.description: Burke argues both that narrowing-of-circumference produces deflective motive-attributions (monetary reduction, behaviorism) AND that 'works of wider circumference [can] give us the faultiest interpretation of a particular motivational cluster' because 'concepts become poorer in contents... in proportion as their extension increases' (p.87). The implied normative rule — choose the *right* circumference — depends on a meta-criterion Burke does not specify.
